Detects file creation inside <temp>\.laravel_locale\ matching the article's exact naming patterns: 12-hex-character .php (the ~5,900-line stealer fetched from flipboxstudio.info/payload) or 8-hex-character .vbs (Windows cscript launcher). Catches the runtime dropper post-detonation, including the marker MD5 file that gates re-execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim path patterns: `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<md5_hash>` (32-hex marker), `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<12 random hex chars>.php` (stealer body), `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<8 random hex chars>.vbs` (Windows launcher). The directory name plus the hex-only filename regex makes near-zero-FP. Cross-checked with https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic tool unpacking a captured sample preserving original directory name
  • Aikido / Socket / Snyk sandbox detonating the IOC on a build agent
  • Security researcher reproducing the dropper for analysis
  • Backup restore of a previously infected host that contains residual .laravel_locale artifacts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm initiating process is php / cscript / wscript / curl / wget — if so the dropper is mid-execution. Capture SHA256 of every file under .laravel_locale and submit to VT/IR sandbox; preserve the .vbs and .php contents to identify which of the 15 stealer modules ran (cloud-creds vs crypto-wallet vs browser-saved-passwords). 2) Contain: kill the cscript/php process tree, isolate host, block flipboxstudio.info DNS/IP, snapshot disk before remediation since the stealer self-deletes. 3) Hunt: assume credential theft completed — rotate every credential the article enumerates (AWS keys + IMDS role, GCP ADC, Azure MSAL cache, DO/Heroku/Vercel/Netlify/Railway/Fly tokens, kubeconfigs, Vault tokens, all SSH keys, .git-credentials, .npmrc/.pypirc/.composer/auth.json, GitHub/GitLab CLI tokens, Slack/Discord/Telegram bot tokens, browser saved passwords across 17 Chromium browsers + Firefox + KeePass + 1Password + Bitwarden, all crypto wallets and seed phrases). Audit AWS CloudTrail / 
let LookbackDays = 14d;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has @".laravel_locale" or FolderPath has @"/.laravel_locale/" or FolderPath has @"\\.laravel_locale\\"
| where (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$")
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$")
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has ".laravel_locale"
| where (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Laravel-Lang Stealer Files Dropped in .laravel_locale Temp Dir
id: 1c8a6e4d-3f72-49bc-9d18-7a2bf0c4e5e9
description: Detects creation of files inside <temp>\.laravel_locale\ matching the Laravel-Lang stealer payload pattern (12-hex .php, 8-hex .vbs, or 32-hex MD5 marker file). Article (Aikido, 22 May 2026) confirms the dropper writes these exact patterns to the system temp directory.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/supply-chain-attack-targets-laravel-lang-packages-with-credential-stealer
  - https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_dir:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.laravel_locale\'
      - '/.laravel_locale/'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|re|i:
      - '\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{12}\.php$'
      - '\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$'
      - '\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{32}$'
  condition: selection_dir and selection_name
falsepositives:
  - None expected; folder name is attacker-specific
level: critical
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.laravel_locale\\* OR */.laravel_locale/*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @file.path:(*/.laravel_locale/*)) OR (source:windows.defender @FilePath:(*\\.laravel_locale\\* OR */.laravel_locale/*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/]/i
| (TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/][0-9a-f]{12}\.php$/i or TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$/i or TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/][0-9a-f]{32}$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.laravel_locale\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.laravel_locale/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.laravel_locale\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.laravel_locale/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action

| where match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:

            - '\Cookies'

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

Megalodon: Mass GitHub Actions Secret Exfiltration Across 5,500+ Public Repositories

A forged commit. A workflow file disguised as a routine CI optimization. Within 6 hours, 5,561 GitHub repositories were backdoored. Cloud credentials harvested. SSH keys stolen. OIDC tokens minted and exfiltrated before any runner finished. The attacker never touched your application code, only your pipeline. Most repositories had no idea it happened.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Megalodon backdoor workflow file (SysDiag.yml / Optimize-Build.yml) written to .github/workflows/ · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Megalodon: Mass GitHub Actions Secret Exfiltration Across 5,500+ Public Reposito
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Megalodon CI/CD exfil: outbound HTTPS to C2 216.126.225.129:8443 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Megalodon harvester: curl POST to C2 /collect endpoint on Linux runner · [LLM] Megalodon harvester: bash secret-grep across workspace (API_KEY|SECRET|TOKEN|PRIVATE_KEY|BEGIN RSA) · [LLM] Megalodon harvester: clustered read of ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.kube/config, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json in one session · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Megalodon CI/CD exfil: outbound HTTPS to C2 216.126.225.129:8443 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host (corporate proxy, EDR-monitored endpoint, self-hosted GitHub Actions runner) initiating a connection to the Megalodon campaign C2 server. The IP/port pair is unique to this campaign and any hit is a near-certain compromise indicator across the org. Rationale: Anchors on the article-published C2 IP 216.126.225.129 — a single hard IOC that StepSecurity attributes directly to the Megalodon campaign. The IP/port combo is not associated with any legitimate service in the article and any internal egress is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1041 T1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red team or IR analyst replaying the IOC for validation
  • Threat-intel platform performing IP reputation/sandbox lookups against the IOC
  • Honeypot or deception infrastructure deliberately calling the IOC to log adversary follow-on
  • CTI researcher in the org pivoting on the IP via VirusTotal/Shodan from a workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("VirusTotalUploader.exe","sandboxie.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--ir-validation"
Response runbook
Triage: pivot DeviceName/SourceIP back to its role — is this a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner, developer workstation that cloned a poisoned repo, or production workload? Pull initiating process and command line; expected pattern is curl POST to /collect. Contain: block 216.126.225.129/32 at egress firewall and proxy; isolate the device in Defender/CrowdStrike; rotate ALL secrets potentially present on the runner (cloud IAM keys, OIDC trust relationships, npm tokens, SSH keys, GitHub PATs, Vault tokens). Treat OIDC token exposure as full cloud-role compromise — re-scope or delete trust policies. Hunt: pivot off the device to UC3 (mass secret grep), UC5 (cred-file fan-out), and search GitHub audit logs for commits authored by build-bot@github-ci.com or ci-pipeline@actions-bot.com on any repo the org owns.

| order by Timestamp desc

Megalodon harvester: curl POST to C2 /collect endpoint on Linux runner AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the runtime exfil step of the Megalodon payload — a curl invocation POSTing gzipped credential blob to https://216.126.225.129:8443/collect. Catches both self-hosted runners and any Linux/Windows host re-executing the decoded payload. Rationale: Pivots on the verbatim exfil command in the article — curl POST to https://216.126.225.129:8443/collect with --data-binary. Combining curl binary + IP + /collect path makes a near-zero-FP detection that catches the payload even if the decoded bash is split across multiple invocations.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1041 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/red-team replaying the public payload on a test runner
  • Reverse-engineer detonating the decoded bash in a sandbox
  • Detection-engineering validation test in non-prod
  • Threat-intel scraper fetching the exact URL
Response runbook
Triage: confirm process tree — initiating bash should be child of a GitHub Actions Runner.Listener / runsvc.sh / runner-worker process for a self-hosted runner, or any sh/bash on a non-runner host. Inspect ProcessCommandLine for the full curl argv (`-X POST`, `--data-binary @-`). Contain: kill the curl PID, isolate host, block 216.126.225.129/32 egress. If a GitHub Actions runner: deregister the runner, revoke its registration token, and rotate the repo/org-level PAT and any OIDC trust relationships exposed. Hunt: same aid/DeviceName — look for preceding bash with base64 -d piping into bash, env dump, ~/.ssh/id_* reads (UC5), and grep with API_KEY/SECRET/TOKEN pattern (UC3). Cross-check GitHub for recent workflow file changes on the repo whose runner fired.

| where FileName =~ "curl" or FileName =~ "curl.exe" or FolderPath endswith "/curl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "216.126.225.129" and ProcessCommandLine has "/collect"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "curl" or ActingProcessName endswith "curl.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "216.126.225.129" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/collect"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Megalodon harvester: bash secret-grep across workspace (API_KEY|SECRET|TOKEN|PRIVATE_KEY|BEGIN RSA) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the recursive secret-scrape step of the Megalodon payload — `grep -rE "(API_KEY|SECRET|TOKEN|PASSWORD|PRIVATE_KEY|BEGIN RSA)"` walking the CI checkout looking for hardcoded secrets. The literal token list is the article-published payload string. Rationale: All six tokens (API_KEY, SECRET, TOKEN, PASSWORD, PRIVATE_KEY, BEGIN RSA) appear verbatim in the published bash payload's grep regex. Requiring all six together discriminates Megalodon from generic secret-scanners (gitleaks/trufflehog use their own ruleset, not raw greps with this exact token list).
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ad-hoc developer secret-audit shell one-liners
  • Custom in-house secret-scanning script using this exact pattern
  • Security training/CTF exercises using this canonical pattern
  • Pre-commit hooks running grep-based secret scans
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitleaks","trufflehog","detect-secrets","semgrep","ggshield") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("gitleaks","trufflehog","--baseline","pre-commit")
Response runbook
Triage: inspect parent process — is this running under a CI runner identity (e.g. `runner`, `gitlab-runner`, `dockerexec`), a service account on a build host, or an interactive user? Megalodon variant always spawns from base64-decoded bash under the runner-worker tree. Contain: if running on a CI runner, terminate the job and deregister the runner. Rotate every secret accessible to that pipeline (cloud IAM, npm tokens, GitHub PATs). Hunt: pivot on same aid/DeviceName for UC1 (egress to C2), UC2 (curl /collect), and UC5 (cred-file fan-out). Check upstream GitHub for recent workflow edits authored by build-bot@github-ci.com or ci-pipeline@actions-bot.com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "grep" or FolderPath endswith "/grep"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("API_KEY", "SECRET", "TOKEN", "PASSWORD", "PRIVATE_KEY", "BEGIN RSA")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "grep"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("API_KEY", "SECRET", "TOKEN", "PASSWORD", "PRIVATE_KEY", "BEGIN RSA")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Megalodon backdoor workflow file (SysDiag.yml / Optimize-Build.yml) written to .github/workflows/ AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a workflow file with one of the two campaign-specific filenames inside any .github/workflows/ directory. Catches developer workstations that cloned/pulled a poisoned repository as well as self-hosted runners checking out the malicious tree. Rationale: Both filenames (SysDiag.yml, Optimize-Build.yml) and the `name:` field values SysDiag / Optimize-Build are called out as the two campaign variants in the article and the recommended GitHub code search anchors. The path scope (.github/workflows/) plus exact filename match make this near-zero-FP.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate project genuinely naming a workflow SysDiag.yml or Optimize-Build.yml — exceedingly rare
  • IR/red-team adding the IOC file to a test repo for detection validation
  • Threat-intel analyst pulling the SafeDep megalodon-campaign-commits.csv reference repo locally
Response runbook
Triage: inspect the file content — confirm the workflow `name:` field is SysDiag or Optimize-Build and the run block contains a base64 blob piped to bash. Cross-reference the repo against SafeDep's megalodon-campaign-commits.csv. Contain: alert the repo owner; revert the malicious commit via `git revert <sha>`; force-pull a clean copy and require branch-protection with mandatory PR reviews on the default branch. If the workflow ever ran on a self-hosted runner, treat all secrets and OIDC trust relationships exposed to that runner as compromised. Hunt: search all org repos for the same two filenames and for commits authored by build-bot@github-ci.com / ci-pipeline@actions-bot.com with messages 'ci: add build optimization step' / 'chore: optimize pipeline runtime' / 'chore: update ci/cd pipeline'.

title: Megalodon Backdoored GitHub Actions Workflow File Written
id: 9d4a7b1e-5f6a-7c8d-ca1b-4e5f6a7b8c9d
description: Detects creation of one of the two named Megalodon campaign workflow files (SysDiag.yml or Optimize-Build.yml) inside any .github/workflows/ directory — these filenames are unique to the campaign per the StepSecurity report.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/megalodon-mass-github-actions-secret-exfiltration-across-5-500-public-repositories
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '.github/workflows/'
      - '.github\workflows\'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '/SysDiag.yml'
      - '\SysDiag.yml'
      - '/Optimize-Build.yml'
      - '\Optimize-Build.yml'
  condition: selection_path and selection_name
falsepositives:
  - Unrelated project that happens to use the same filename — vanishingly rare
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\.github\\workflows\\SysDiag.yml OR *\.github\\workflows\\Optimize-Build.yml OR *\.github\/workflows\/SysDiag.yml OR *\.github\/workflows\/Optimize-Build.yml)) OR (source:linux.auditd @file.path:(*\.github\/workflows\/SysDiag.yml OR *\.github\/workflows\/Optimize-Build.yml))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.github[\/\\]workflows[\/\\](SysDiag|Optimize-Build)\.yml$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*.github/workflows/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.github\\workflows\\*") (Filesystem.file_name="SysDiag.yml" OR Filesystem.file_name="Optimize-Build.yml") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*.github/workflows/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.github\\workflows\\*") (Filesystem.file_name="SysDiag.yml" OR Filesystem.file_name="Optimize-Build.yml") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Megalodon harvester: clustered read of ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.kube/config, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json in one session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the credential-collection fan-out pattern — a single process tree reading multiple distinct credential stores (SSH private key, kube config, npm token, Docker registry creds) within a one-minute window. Catches Megalodon even if the bash one-liner is split into separate cat invocations and the C2 IP is not yet contactable. Rationale: Anchors directly on the article's decoded payload (Code blocks 2 and 3) — the exact targets cat'd by the Megalodon harvester: /proc/1/environ, ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.kube/config, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json. Requiring ≥3 distinct targets from the same parent within 1 minute discriminates from any single legitimate dotfile-reading tool.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Chef/Puppet provisioning role enumerating user credentials
  • Container-image bake script copying user dotfiles into an image
  • Backup agent (restic, borg) walking $HOME
  • Developer running `dotfiles install` or similar bootstrap script
  • Kubernetes/cloud SDK install scripts merging multiple credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-call","restic","borg","rsync") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","--inventory","site.pp","chef-solo")
Response runbook
Triage: identify parent process. Megalodon harvester runs under a child of the GitHub Actions runner-worker (Runner.Worker / runsvc.sh) or under a base64-decoded bash. A legitimate config-management tool will run as ansible/puppet/chef child of cron or sshd. Contain: if on a CI runner, terminate the job, deregister the runner, rotate all secrets in scope of the pipeline. Rotate SSH keys read; revoke npm tokens; cycle kube config service-account tokens; rotate Docker registry creds. Hunt: pivot on same DeviceName for UC1 (egress to 216.126.225.129) and UC2 (curl /collect). Look for preceding `bash -c "echo <base64> | base64 -d | bash"` invocation. Audit GitHub for matching workflow file additions in the org.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMin = 1m;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName =~ "cat" or FolderPath endswith "/cat"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/proc/1/environ","/.ssh/id_","/.kube/config","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json")
| extend Target = case(
    ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/1/environ","pid1_env",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.ssh/id_","ssh_key",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.kube/config","kube",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.npmrc","npm",
    ProcessCommandLine has "/.docker/config.json","docker",
    "")
| summarize
    DistinctTargets = dcount(Target),
    Targets = make_set(Target, 10),
    SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
    LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, WindowMin)
| where DistinctTargets >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMin = 1m;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "cat"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/proc/1/environ","/.ssh/id_","/.kube/config","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json")
| extend Target = case(
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/1/environ","pid1_env",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.ssh/id_","ssh_key",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.kube/config","kube",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.npmrc","npm",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "/.docker/config.json","docker",
    "")
| summarize
    DistinctTargets = dcount(Target),
    Targets = make_set(Target, 10),
    SampleCmds = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMin)
| where DistinctTargets >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.auditd @process.executable.path:*\/cat @process.command_line:(*\/proc\/1\/environ* OR *\/.ssh\/id_* OR *\/.kube\/config* OR *\/.npmrc* OR *\/.docker\/config.json*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/cat$/i CommandLine=/(\/proc\/1\/environ|\/\.ssh\/id_|\/\.kube\/config|\/\.npmrc|\/\.docker\/config\.json)/
| case {
    CommandLine=/\/proc\/1\/environ/ | target := "pid1";
    CommandLine=/\/\.ssh\/id_/ | target := "ssh";
    CommandLine=/\/\.kube\/config/ | target := "kube";
    CommandLine=/\/\.npmrc/ | target := "npm";
    CommandLine=/\/\.docker\/config\.json/ | target := "docker";
  }
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName], function=[count(field=target, distinct=true, as=distinct_targets), collect([target])])
| distinct_targets >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cat (Processes.process="*/proc/1/environ*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh/id_*" OR Processes.process="*/.kube/config*" OR Processes.process="*/.npmrc*" OR Processes.process="*/.docker/config.json*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval is_ssh=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.ssh/id_"),1,0), is_kube=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.kube/config"),1,0), is_npm=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.npmrc"),1,0), is_proc=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/proc/1/environ"),1,0), is_docker=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.docker/config.json"),1,0) | eval distinct_targets=is_ssh+is_kube+is_npm+is_proc+is_docker | where distinct_targets>=3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=cat (Processes.process="*/proc/1/environ*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh/id_*" OR Processes.process="*/.kube/config*" OR Processes.process="*/.npmrc*" OR Processes.process="*/.docker/config.json*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval is_ssh=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.ssh/id_"),1,0), is_kube=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.kube/config"),1,0), is_npm=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.npmrc"),1,0), is_proc=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/proc/1/environ"),1,0), is_docker=if(match(mvjoin(cmds,"|"),"/.docker/config.json"),1,0) | eval distinct_targets=is_ssh+is_kube+is_npm+is_proc+is_docker | where distinct_targets>=3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or SHA1 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or MD5 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or SHA1 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or MD5 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mail-borne click to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing domain AIDelivery High
Detects users clicking links in email that resolve to known FIFA World Cup 2026 typosquat domains (fifa26.shop, *26-fifa.com and lookalike patterns). Pivots on Safe Links / email URL telemetry to catch the delivery vector before credential entry. Rationale: Uses the article's named IOC fifa26.shop plus the second sample family `*26-fifa[.]com`, expanded to a typosquat regex covering common .shop/.store TLDs the article explicitly calls out. Explicit allow for legitimate fifa.com prevents official-site collisions. Cross-checked: WHOIS/abuse.ch lookups for typosquat campaigns around major sporting events show recurring `<event>+<year>+.shop` patterns. Sentinel rewritten to use ImWebSession (EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo are M365D-only and not in this tenant's Sentinel schema). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate fan news sites or blogs whose path contains 'fifa' and '2026'
  • Official FIFA marketing redirects through partner shorteners
  • Sports journalists researching scam sites for stories
  • Security researchers / TI analysts visiting the IOCs for triage
  • Sponsored ad clicks to FIFA official partners on non-.fifa.com domains (e.g. ticketing resellers explicitly authorised by FIFA)
Suppression filter
| where not (Url matches regex @'(?i)://(www\.)?fifa\.com(/|$)') and not (HttpHostName endswith 'fifa.com') and not (HttpHostName in~ ('store.fifa.com','tickets.fifa.com','hospitality.fifa.com'))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URL host is not a legitimate FIFA partner (FIFA's only official ticketing channels are fifa.com/tickets, fifa.com/hospitality, and the Qatar Airways travel packages). Pull the originating email (NetworkMessageId) or referrer to identify delivery vector. 2) Contain: block the typosquat domain at proxy/DNS and Safe Links, purge any related emails via M365 Threat Explorer, force password reset + revoke sessions for the clicking user (article confirms credential + card harvesting). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user's last 24h for additional FIFA-themed clicks, look for outbound POSTs to the same host (likely contains exfiltrated card data), and scan EmailUrlInfo for the same UrlDomain across other recipients in the org.
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
let ClickedUrls = UrlClickEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where ActionType in ('ClickAllowed','ClickedThrough','UrlScanInProgress')
  | where Url matches regex TyposquatRegex or parse_url(Url).Host has_any (KnownBad)
  | where not (Url matches regex @'(?i)://(www\.)?fifa\.com(/|$)');
ClickedUrls
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | project NetworkMessageId, UrlDomain, MailUrl=Url) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, MailUrl, UrlDomain, ActionType, ThreatTypes, NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough
| order by Timestamp desc
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(Url)
| where Url matches regex TyposquatRegex or HttpHostName has_any (KnownBad)
| where not (Url matches regex @'(?i)://(www\.)?fifa\.com(/|$)') and not (HttpHostName endswith 'fifa.com')
| extend MailReferrer = iif(HttpRequestHeaderReferer matches regex @'(?i)(outlook|mail\.google|webmail|owa|m365|office\.com)', true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, MailReferrer, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Click or Navigation to Fake FIFA World Cup 2026 Typosquat Domain
id: 7c0e1f4a-8a6f-4f3d-9b1a-2f8c1d3e4b91
description: Detects browser navigation to known fake FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing domains and typosquat patterns reported by ESET.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:

  - attack.t1583.001

  category: proxy
detection:
  selection_known:
    c-uri|contains:

  selection_pattern:

  filter_legit:

  - Legitimate fan blogs or news sites with 'fifa' and '2026' in the URL path
  - Marketing redirects from official FIFA partners

#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site|com)/ OR DomainName=/(?i)^(fifa26\.shop|26-fifa\.com)$/
| NOT DomainName=/(?i)\.fifa\.com$|^fifa\.com$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])

Endpoint DNS or web traffic to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 typosquat domain AIDelivery High
Detects endpoint DNS resolution or outbound web connection to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing infrastructure (fifa26.shop, *26-fifa.com pattern) regardless of delivery vector — catches users reaching the site via sponsored search, social-media ads, or shared chat links. Rationale: Direct DNS/web pivot using the two domain families named in the article (fifa26.shop and *26-fifa.com), expanded to a tight typosquat regex bounded by the .shop/.store/.online TLDs the article specifically calls out as a red flag. Browser-process filter on the Defender side suppresses background DNS noise. Cross-checked against MITRE T1583.001 (typosquatting subtechnique). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1566.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel / DFIR analysts resolving the IOC during triage from a managed workstation
  • Web crawlers or threat-intel scrapers running in the org's environment
  • Marketing or PR staff researching the campaign for brand-protection write-ups
  • Fan-blog hostnames that legitimately contain 'fifa' + '2026' (rare but possible on .com)
  • Sandbox/VM detonations of malicious URLs from a corporate analyst host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountUpn !in~ ('soc-analyst@contoso.com','threat-intel@contoso.com') and DeviceName !startswith 'SOC-SANDBOX-'
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting process and user — if it's a browser session by a regular employee (not SOC/TI), treat as a real visit; pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId in a ±30min window to see if any POST traffic followed the resolution (indicates credential or card submission). 2) Contain: sinkhole the domain at recursive DNS / block at proxy + Safe Links, isolate device if POST traffic to the typosquat is confirmed, force password reset and card cancellation for the affected user. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host in the org that resolved any matching FIFA typosquat domain in the last 30d, query EmailUrlInfo for the same domains to size the delivery footprint, and pivot on shared resolved IPs to discover sibling typosquat infrastructure on the same hosting.
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site|com)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host))
| where Host has_any (KnownBad) or Host matches regex TyposquatRegex
| where not (Host endswith 'fifa.com') and Host != 'fifa.com'
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ('chrome.exe','msedge.exe','firefox.exe','brave.exe','opera.exe','iexplore.exe','safari.exe')
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, Host, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site|com)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Name has_any (KnownBad) or Name matches regex TyposquatRegex
    | where not (Name endswith 'fifa.com') and Name != 'fifa.com'
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, QueryName=Name, QueryType=QueryTypeName, Result, Source='DnsEvents'),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DnsQuery has_any (KnownBad) or DnsQuery matches regex TyposquatRegex
    | where not (DnsQuery endswith 'fifa.com') and DnsQuery != 'fifa.com'
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, QueryName=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, Result=DnsResponseName, Source='ImDnsActivity')
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to Fake FIFA World Cup 2026 Typosquat Domain
id: 9a4b2d1e-5c8f-4e2a-bb7c-1a9d4e6f2c83
description: Detects DNS resolution of FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing typosquat domains reported by ESET (fifa26.shop and the *26-fifa.com family).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybersecurity/foul-play-fake-fifa-world-cup-websites-tickets/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:

  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection_known:
    QueryName|contains:
      - 'fifa26.shop'
      - '26-fifa.com'
      - '26-fifa.'
  selection_pattern:
    QueryName|re|i: '(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site)'
  filter_legit:
    QueryName|endswith:
      - '.fifa.com'
      - 'fifa.com'
  condition: (selection_known or selection_pattern) and not filter_legit
level: high
falsepositives:
  - Security researchers querying the IOC for analysis
  - Legitimate fan sites with 'fifa' and '2026' in the hostname
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22) AND (@QueryName:(*fifa26.shop* OR *26-fifa.* OR *26fifa.* OR fifa*worldcup*.shop OR fifa*worldcup*.store)) AND NOT @QueryName:(*.fifa.com OR fifa.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(?i)^(fifa26\.shop|.*26-fifa\..*|.*26fifa\.(shop|store))$/ OR DomainName=/(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site)/
| NOT DomainName=/(?i)(^|\.)fifa\.com$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, IpAddress], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.answer) as answer from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*.fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.com" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.*" OR DNS.query="*26fifa.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.store") AND NOT (DNS.query="*.fifa.com" OR DNS.query="fifa.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.answer) as answer from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*.fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.com" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.*" OR DNS.query="*26fifa.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.store") AND NOT (DNS.query="*.fifa.com" OR DNS.query="fifa.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"

5 Supply Chain Attacks in 48 Hours: Why Securing One Layer Is Not Enough

StepSecurity
2026-05-21 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A poisoned VS Code extension breached GitHub. A trojanized PyPI package hit Microsoft. Compromised GitHub Actions and a self-spreading npm worm targeted thousands more. In just 48 hours, attackers hit every layer of the software development pipeline. Traditional security tools did not stop any of it.

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Known Shai-Hulud / Nx Console implant hash match (SHA256/SHA1) · [LLM] macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist persistence pointing at Python interpreter · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Nx Console / Shai-Hulud C2 connection (t.m-kosche.com, check.git-service.com, filev2.getsession.org, api.masscan.cloud, 83.142.209.194) · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Developer credential store read by Python or Node spawned from VS Code (Nx Console stealer pattern) · [LLM] GitHub audit log bulk private-repo clone burst (post Nx Console compromise pattern)
Compromised Nx Console VS Code extension (nrwl.angular-console v18.94.0/18.95.0/18.100.0) install on endpoint AIDelivery High
Detects writes/installations of the malicious Nx Console extension versions published to the VS Code Marketplace on May 18, 2026. Initial-access pivot for the Shai-Hulud / TeamPCP supply-chain campaign that compromised a GitHub employee laptop and led to ~3,800 internal repos being exfiltrated. Rationale: Targets the exact malicious extension version strings from the StepSecurity article (cross-referenced against Wiz, Socket.dev, and JFrog vendor write-ups in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287); developer endpoints almost never receive a freshly published Nx Console version within hours of release so the temporal-uniqueness of these specific versions makes this very low FP. We also covered the two neighbour versions (18.94.0 / 18.100.0) StepSecurity flagged as also impacted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher pulling the malicious extension into a sandbox VM for reverse engineering
  • Threat intel team mirroring the marketplace artifact for IOC enrichment
  • Internal red team replaying the attack chain in a purple-team exercise
  • An internal cache/proxy snapshot of the marketplace replaying the old version metadata on backup restore
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("redteam@contoso.com","malware-lab@contoso.com")) and not (DeviceName startswith "SANDBOX-" or DeviceName startswith "REVENG-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for the device for ±2h around the install; confirm the file SHA matches one of the known stealer hashes (see UC2) and that VS Code's Code Helper is the writing process. Pull DeviceInfo to identify whether the user is a developer / engineering org member. 2. Contain: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response (or MDM); revoke all GitHub PATs, SSH keys, AWS access keys, npm tokens for the user; force AAD/Okta password+MFA reset; remove the extension via `code --uninstall-extension nrwl.angular-console`. 3. Hunt: Sweep the org for any other device that ever installed nrwl.angular-console between 2026-05-18 and 2026-05-20; pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs) and UC6 (bulk GitHub clones from this user) to scope post-exploitation activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or FileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","code","code-helper","Code.exe")
    or FolderPath has_any (".vscode/extensions","\\.vscode\\extensions\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or TargetFileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Shai-Hulud / Nx Console implant hash match (SHA256/SHA1) AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based catch-all for the 8 SHA256 and 7 SHA1 implant artifacts attributed to the May 2026 Nx Console / TeamPCP supply-chain attack. Fires whether the artifact is written to disk, loaded as a module, or executed as a process. Rationale: Hashes drawn directly from the StepSecurity pre-extracted IOC bundle for the article (corroborated against Wiz, Datadog, and JFrog vendor analyses in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1285). Hash matches are essentially zero-FP on production endpoints; the union across process/file/image-load tables catches the implant whether it's executed, dropped, or sideloaded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reverse-engineering sandbox VM detonating the sample
  • CrowdStrike/Defender threat-hunt team replaying the artifact for IOC tuning
  • Backup-restore replay of a quarantined Defender sample triggering a re-scan
  • Malware-museum / IR-training lab images carrying the hash in a vault
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "SANDBOX-" or DeviceName startswith "REVENG-" or DeviceName startswith "MWLAB-") and not (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("redteam@contoso.com","malware-lab@contoso.com"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm host is a real production endpoint (not a sandbox via DeviceInfo.DeviceCategory / device naming); correlate with UC1 to determine if the malicious extension was the entry vector; pull the parent process chain to map the kill chain. 2. Contain: Isolate via Defender network-isolation; rotate every credential the user touched in last 30d (GitHub PATs, SSH keys, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, Okta/AAD password, AAD refresh tokens via revokeSignInSessions); for macOS hosts also revoke iCloud Keychain access. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs), UC4 (LaunchAgent persistence) and UC6 (GitHub bulk clones) using the same UPN/AccountUpn; sweep the device images directory for any other extension installed within 48h of the malicious one — TeamPCP have shown ability to bundle multiple compromised IDE extensions.

Nx Console / Shai-Hulud C2 connection (t.m-kosche.com, check.git-service.com, filev2.getsession.org, api.masscan.cloud, 83.142.209.194) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network or DNS activity to any of the 4 known C2 domains or the dedicated IP used by the May 2026 Nx Console credential stealer. Covers HTTPS exfil, GitHub-API-shaped C2 (api.masscan.cloud), and the resolver side of DNS tunneling. Rationale: All 4 domains and the IP are first-source listed in the StepSecurity article and triple-corroborated against Wiz, Socket.dev, and Datadog write-ups (session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287). t.m-kosche.com is the shared C2 across every layer of the Shai-Hulud campaign — a single hit is unambiguous. We also catch subdomain variations because the DNS-tunneling channel hides data in TXT-query subdomains beneath api.masscan.cloud. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the IOC to confirm site is offline
  • Sinkhole/passive-DNS infrastructure resolving the domain
  • Network sandbox detonation of the sample replaying C2 callouts
  • Internal honeypot relay that intentionally resolves known-bad domains for tracking
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","safari") and InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("threatintel@contoso.com","soc-analyst@contoso.com"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the initiating process — if it's `Code Helper`, `node`, or `python` on a developer endpoint, treat as critical and pivot directly to UC1 (extension install) and UC2 (hash match). Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the device for ±24h to spot longer C2 cadence. 2. Contain: Sinkhole all 4 domains at corporate DNS; null-route 83.142.209.194 at the edge; isolate the originating endpoint via Defender; revoke all credentials accessible from the device. 3. Hunt: Sweep DNS logs across the whole org for the last 30d for any other host that resolved these domains, even once; pivot to GitHub audit logs (UC6) for the affected user looking for repo-clone bursts during the C2 window.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com","check.git-service.com","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and (RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains))) or (RemoteIP in (C2IPs))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="DNS", IndicatorMatched=DnsQuery
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) or Url has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="Network", IndicatorMatched=coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains) or DestinationIP in (C2IPs) or RequestURL has_any (C2Domains)

   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, IndicatorMatched, Source)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist persistence pointing at Python interpreter AIInstallation Medium
Detects creation of a LaunchAgent / LaunchDaemon plist in the typical macOS auto-start locations whose plist content references a python interpreter — the persistence mechanism used by the Nx Console implant to keep the credential stealer alive across reboots on the GitHub employee's laptop. Rationale: Persistence detail comes directly from the kill-chain Phase 3 hint and the article's explicit 'Persistent Python backdoor installed on macOS' claim. Filtering the writer process to VS Code / node / python is the key noise reducer — legitimate apps installing LaunchAgents are almost always the app binary itself (Spotify, Docker, etc.), not an interpreter. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1547.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a self-built Python service via launchctl
  • Homebrew tap that registers a python-based daemon (e.g. supervisord, redis-helper-py)
  • VS Code extension legitimately registering a background helper (rare but happens for language servers)
  • Apple/Anaconda installer creating ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.anaconda.kickstart.plist on first run
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("com.spotify.","com.docker.","com.apple.","com.anaconda.","homebrew.","org.jenkins-ci."))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Cat the plist contents (or grab via Defender Live Response): `launchctl list | grep <label>` and `plutil -p <plist>`; check if `ProgramArguments` references a python script under `~/.vscode/extensions/nrwl.angular-console-*` or `~/Library/Application Support/Code/`. 2. Contain: `launchctl unload <plist>` and quarantine the plist + referenced script; isolate the host; revoke developer credentials. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC2 (hash match) on the referenced python script; pull DeviceProcessEvents for any python child of Code/Code Helper across the org in the last 30d; check `~/Library/LaunchAgents/` on every macOS engineering laptop for plists installed since 2026-05-18.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceName !contains "win-" // narrow to macOS heuristically; or join DeviceInfo where OSPlatform == "macOS"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","node","python","python3","bash","zsh","sh")
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("python","python3","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode/extensions")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where OSPlatform == "macOS" or isempty(OSPlatform)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".plist"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","node","python","python3","bash","zsh")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("python","python3","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode/extensions")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: macOS LaunchAgent Persistence via VS Code Helper or Python (Nx Console Implant)

Developer credential store read by Python or Node spawned from VS Code (Nx Console stealer pattern) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for reads of GitHub/AWS/SSH/npm credential files or macOS Keychain by a python or node process whose parent (or grand-parent) is VS Code's Code Helper — the exact telemetry shape generated by the Nx Console multi-stage credential stealer. Rationale: Cross-table pivot covering Phase 4 (credential_access) — the article explicitly calls out 'Multi-stage credential stealer' targeting developer secrets. Threshold of ≥2 distinct credential paths per session strips legitimate single-file dev workflows (e.g. python reading its own ~/.ssh for git push) while preserving the stealer's signature of sweeping every secret store in one pass. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package
ATT&CKT1555 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / Terraform invoked via python that legitimately reads ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh/config
  • npm postinstall scripts that probe ~/.npmrc for auth tokens during legitimate package install
  • DevOps tooling like aws-sso-util refreshing creds across .aws/ and .config/
  • macOS Keychain Access utilities (osascript wrappers) inventoried by IT compliance scans
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","terraform","aws-sso-util","aws-vault","saml2aws","chamber","keybase"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the full process tree for the InitiatingProcessId — confirm parent chain leads back to Code/Code Helper and the cwd is inside `~/.vscode/extensions/nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0/` (or the 94/100 variants). Inspect the python script content if recoverable. 2. Contain: Isolate device; rotate every credential the python process touched — for SSH keys revoke from GitHub immediately, for AWS keys disable in IAM, for npm tokens revoke in npmjs, for gh tokens use `gh auth refresh`. Force AAD password reset and revoke refresh tokens. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs) to see if creds were exfiltrated, and to UC6 (GitHub clone bursts) under the same user. Sweep the org for any other developer whose VS Code spawned python reading ≥2 credential paths in 30d.
let CredentialPaths = dynamic(["/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.ssh/id_ecdsa","/.ssh/config","/.ssh/known_hosts","/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","/.config/gh/config.yml","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json","/.kube/config","/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db","/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies","/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Login Data","/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Cookies"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileAccessed","FileOpened")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","node","osascript")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredentialPaths) or FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","hosts.yml",".npmrc","login.keychain-db")
| extend ParentIsVSCode = InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","code","code-helper","Code.exe")
| extend FromExtensionDir = InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vscode/extensions","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode-server/extensions")
| where ParentIsVSCode or FromExtensionDir
| summarize FilesTouched = make_set(strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName), 50), FileCount = dcount(strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SamplePid = any(InitiatingProcessId), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| where FileCount >= 2 // distinct credential files reads in same session ≫ single-file dev workflow
| order by FileCount desc
let CredentialPaths = dynamic(["/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.ssh/config","/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json","/.kube/config","/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db","/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("python","python3","node","osascript")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredentialPaths) or TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","hosts.yml",".npmrc")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vscode/extensions","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode-server/extensions") 
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has "Code Helper"
| summarize FilesTouched = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50), FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where FileCount >= 2
| order by FileCount desc
